newsitem.title: CANADA: Officials ponder fate of Sable Island project.
newsitem.headline: Officials ponder fate of Sable Island project.

text.p: Canadian regulators are pondering the fate of the C$3 billion Sable Island off-shore natural gas project following three months of hearings and continuing political wrangling.

The hearings before a joint federal-provincial review panel ended this week much the way they began, with squabbles about shipping charges and over the proposed route for the pipeline that would carry the gas to markets in eastern Canada and the U.S. Northeast.

The five-member panel led by the National Energy Board is expected to make its recommendation by September to the Canadian government on the Mobil Oil Canada -led project and the allied pipeline proposal.

The project -- which is also part owned by Shell Canada Ltd, Imperial Oil Ltd and Nova Scotia Resources Ltd -- would drill in the Atlantic Ocean 200 km east of Nova Scotia. The area is believed to have reserves of about three trillion cubic feet (84.95 billion cubic metres).

Nova Scotia's premier-elect Russell MacLellan, who will be sworn in this week, caused a last-minute uproar when he complained to regulators that a previously agreed plan would result in higher electricity costs in his province. MacLellan announced he wanted to renegotiate a rate plan worked out midway through the hearings by Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Maritimes & Northeast Pipeline.

The pipeline is owned by Mobil, Westcoast Energy Inc and PanEnergy Corp The pipeline had proposed charging the provinces the same rate, but agreed to give Nova Scotia a 10 percent discount for eight years and four percent for two years. New Brunswick would get a four percent reduction for three years.

MacLellan, who contends that Nova Scotia is still not being properly reimbursed for the use of its natural gas resource, proposed the province get a 20 percent price advantage over New Brunswick for the life of the project.
The NEB panel will decide the shipping toll issue.

Equally intense has been the fight between Maritimes & Northeast -- which wants to reach the Boston-area market via Maine -- and a rival plan by Trans-Quebec and Maritimes pipeline (TQM) to ship the gas to Montreal before it goes to the United States.

TQM, which is owned by TransCanada PipeLines Ltd and Gaz Metropolitain and Co LP, has yet to submit a formal proposal,but used the hearings to argue a decision on a pipeline route should be delayed until both plans are considered.

Mobil officials have warned that any delays in approving either the drilling or pipeline would force them to scuttle the entire proposal because they would not be able to sell in the U.S. markets in a timely fashion.
